content: Tropomyosin alpha-1 chain, also known as TPM1, is a protein encoded by the TPM1 gene in humans. This gene belongs to the tropomyosin (Tm) family, which consists of highly conserved and widely distributed actin-binding proteins. These proteins play a critical role in the contractile systems of both striated and smooth muscles, as well as in the cytoskeleton of non-muscle cells. The TPM1 protein has a molecular weight of approximately 7 kDa and is composed of 284 amino acids. Tropomyosin is a flexible protein that exists as either a homodimer or a heterodimer, consisting of two alpha-helical chains. These chains adopt a bent coiled-coil conformation, which allows them to wrap around seven actin molecules within a functional unit of muscle. Tropomyosin polymerizes end-to-end along the two grooves of actin filaments, providing structural stability to the filaments. In human striated muscles, proteins encoded by the TPM1 (α-Tm), TPM2 (β-Tm), and TPM3 (γ-Tm) genes are expressed. Among these, α-Tm is the predominant isoform in striated muscle. In human cardiac muscle, the ratio of α-Tm to β-Tm is approximately 5:1. Tropomyosin functions in conjunction with the troponin complex to regulate the calcium-dependent interaction between actin and myosin during muscle contraction. Tropomyosin molecules are arranged head-to-tail along the actin thin filament and are essential for the cooperative activation of muscle contraction. A three-state model, proposed by McKillop and Geeves, describes the positions of tropomyosin during the cardiac cycle. 1. In the blocked (B) state, which occurs during diastole when intracellular calcium levels are low, tropomyosin blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin. 2. In the closed (C) state, tropomyosin is positioned on the inner groove of actin. In this state, myosin heads are in a cocked position, weakly bound to actin, and not generating force. 3. In the myosin-binding (M) state, tropomyosin is further displaced from actin by strongly bound myosin cross-bridges that are actively generating force. In addition to binding actin, tropomyosin also binds to troponin T (TnT). Troponin T anchors the region of head-to-tail overlap between adjacent tropomyosin molecules to actin, ensuring proper alignment and function. Mutations in the TPM1 gene have been linked to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). HCM-associated mutations tend to cluster around the N-terminal region and a primary actin-binding region known as period 5. These mutations can disrupt the normal function of tropomyosin, leading to pathological changes in cardiac muscle structure and function.
